content.title: Africa
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text: Lesson 3 Overview

Africa is a continent of 54 countries. The UNDP Regional Bureau for Africa consists of 46 countries with the other eight considered in the Regional Bureau for the Arab States.

Africa stands at a critical turning point where its abundant natural resources, young and growing population, and global shift toward renewable energy present immense opportunities for sustainable development.

Despite its current energy challenges, Africa has:
Vast renewable energy potential and a rich reserve of critical minerals (like cobalt, lithium, and rare earth elements) that are vital to the global clean energy transition.
A strategic opportunity to leapfrog to modern, green energy systems, closing the electricity and clean cooking access gaps that affect over 900 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa.
The chance to create inclusive, low-carbon economies, enabling job creation, skills development, and industrialization while prioritizing gender equality and youth empowerment.

This lesson discusses the African context by exploring Africa’s energy and economic situation. Furthermore, it highlights the development focus for the region, having discussed it’s particular challenges.

content.title: A: Development Context in Africa

content.text: Africa’s rural-urban divide presents a major challenge to sustainable development, particularly in the energy sector. While urban areas increasingly benefit from grid connectivity and infrastructure investments, rural communities remain disproportionately underserved—over 80% of people without electricity in sub-Saharan Africa live in rural areas. This imbalance hinders poverty reduction, limits access to education and healthcare, and exacerbates migration pressures toward cities. Addressing this divide is critical for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 7 on affordable and clean energy.
80% of people without electricity in sub-Saharan Africa live in rural areas
By 2050, Africa is projected to account for 25% of the world’s population.

content.title: Africa offers some of the highest returns on renewable energy investments globally (IRENA, 2022)
content.body: With strong governance and climate finance, Africa is not just a future energy market—it is the frontier of energy growth.

content.title: Over 60% of Africa’s population is under 25
content.body: Yet youth unemployment remains high and technical skills are lacking. Addressing this skills gap through vocational training, technical education, and green innovation hubs will be essential to enable youth and marginalized groups to fully participate in and benefit from the renewable energy transition.

content.title: B: Energy Challenges in Africa

content.text: In this region alone, 571 million people live without electricity, representing 83% of the global electricity access deficit.
Access to clean cooking in Sub-Saharan Africa is a critical and urgent issue.

content.body: Notably, 62% of the world’s poor now live in Sub-Saharan Africa’s resource-rich economies, a sharp rise from 13% in 2000, highlighting that fossil fuel dependence has not led to inclusive or sustained development. Although recent geopolitical events, like the energy crisis from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have temporarily boosted African gas demand, this is not a long-term fix.

In these nations, oil and gas make up over 85% of export earnings, leaving their economies vulnerable to global market fluctuations. Despite this wealth, human development remains low in many fossil fuel-rich countries, such as Chad (HDI 0.394), Republic of Congo (0.479), Nigeria (0.535), and Tanzania (0.549).

content.text: Africa’s economy remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels with 12 countries holding proven oil reserves—Libya, Nigeria, and Angola alone account for about 5% of global reserves.

content.body: Additionally, fossil fuel extraction in Africa is 15-20% more costly and 70-80% more carbon-intensive than elsewhere, increasing risks of stranded assets as global fossil fuel demand falls and debts rise.

Processing operations are primarily concentrated in China, accounting for 35% of nickel, 50-70% of lithium, and cobalt, and 90% of rare earth elements. For instance, Zimbabwe, the sixth-largest global lithium producer, could potentially supply up to 20% of the global lithium market, but currently only accounts for 1% of global lithium supply.

content.title: C: Energy Opportunities in Africa

content.text: Africa’s role in the global economy could be redefined

76% of Africa’s electricity generation could be renewable by 2040, if the right investments and policy frameworks are adopted (IRENA, 2021).
Africa holds 30% of the world’s essential minerals required for renewable technologies such as lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements - critical for batteries, wind turbines, and solar panels (IEA, 2023).
The continent also possesses 60% of the world’s best solar resources, making it uniquely positioned to become a global renewable energy leader (IRENA, 2022).

This clean energy potential could redefine Africa’s role in the global economy - transforming it from an exporter of raw resources into a hub of green industrialization, innovation, and resilience.
Africa need more installed electricity capacity

Currently, Africa’s installed electricity capacity stands at 369 gigawatts (GW)—only 16% of China’s capacity. The average per capita electricity consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa is a mere 200 kWh per year, barely enough to power a few lightbulbs and a small fan. For comparison, China’s consumption is 4,500 kWh, India’s is 1,300 kWh, and Brazil’s is 2,360 kWh. Experts estimate that at least 1,000 kWh per person per year is needed to sustain a path of productive economic development.


Although progress has been made over the past decades, much more needs to be done, especially to obtain a normal and not skewed distribution between the states in the region - South Africa and Egypt alone account for nearly 50% of total electricity production in the region. Off-Grid and Decentralized Power are game changers

With over 80% of Africa’s unelectrified population in rural areas, off-grid solar, mini-grids, and battery storage systems are game changers.

Companies like M-KOPA and d.light are already reaching millions of households with pay-as-you-go solar kits.
Decentralized energy systems can bypass the cost and time of grid extension, offering faster, cleaner access to power.

These solutions create opportunities for local entrepreneurship, digital payments, and financial inclusion..

content.title: D: Energy Strategy in Africa

content.text: Financial investment is critical

To achieve universal energy access by 2030, Africa must secure $25 billion in annual investments.

Yet, between 2000 and 2020, the continent attracted just 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewables, highlighting a significant financing gap.

Scaling up energy finance is not only essential for climate goals but is also a development priority, especially as fossil-fuel-dependent economies face increasing risks. Renewable energy offers Africa a chance to diversify economically, foster resilience, and transition to a digital, climate-smart economy.
African Union Agenda

The AU’s Agenda 2063 already sets an ambitious aspiration to realize

“a prosperous Africa based on inclusive growth and sustainable development”.

This vision is rooted in the need to deliver energy security through interconnected infrastructure and a shift towards “modern, efficient, reliable, cost-effective, renewable and environmentally friendly” energy systems.
Industrial and Supply Chain Development

Africa’s mineral wealth, if harnessed responsibly, can form the backbone of local and regional manufacturing:

Countries like the DRC (70% of global cobalt) and Zimbabwe (significant lithium reserves) can establish local processing and battery manufacturing industries.
Regional supply chains can be developed for solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and electric vehicles, fueling local economies and reducing import dependency.

This would move Africa up the value chain, away from raw exports and towards job-rich, high-value production, attracting foreign direct investment.
Regional cooperation can make energy solutions more cost effective.

Initiatives such as the West African Power Pool, which cover 14 out of 15 countries in the region’s economic block, attempts to integrate national power systems into a unified regional electricity market.
